summary:
Oman criminalises same-sex conduct under the 2018 Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018), with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment; the offence applies to both men and women, and prosecution may proceed without a prior complaint where the act causes a public scandal. A trans visitor in a relationship that Omani law would class as same-sex falls within the same exposure.

Gender expression itself is an offence target. Article 266 of the Penal Law covers impersonating the opposite sex and entering women-only venues while disguised, carrying 1 month to 1 year's imprisonment, and Article 266(d) is the provision through which gender non-conformity is punished. Article 265 covers public indecency (10 days to 3 months plus a fine of OMR 100 to 300), and Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content judged to violate public morals, offline and online, with penalties of up to 1 year and 10 days to 1 month respectively. The Cyber Crime Law 2011 (Articles 17 and 31) has also been used against LGBT expression, carrying 1 month to 3 years plus a fine of OMR 100 to 3,000.

Enforcement against gender-nonconforming people is documented. In January 2018 the Royal Oman Police arrested a group of men in Salalah for dressing as women after photographs circulated on social media; in September 2018 a Salalah preliminary court sentenced two of them to four years' imprisonment and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing the photos, and two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video. In July 2020 the Royal Oman Police announced arrests of 'men in women's clothing' after Snapchat photographs from a private Salalah party circulated, and separately arrested an Asian expat wearing an abaya and niqab during a women-only park hour at Al Buraimi. Human Rights Watch wrote to Omani authorities on 13 July 2020 about these arrests and convictions under the 'imitating the opposite sex' provision. The most recent documented enforcement instance in this record is from July 2020; no later case is documented here.

Border treatment of visibly gender-nonconforming visitors is documented first-hand. On 27 February 2023 a genderqueer/non-binary Indian model-activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa reported that friends cleared immigration while she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt, and touched inappropriately by officers.

Prosecution risk is heightened by digital evidence and surveillance. Article 49 of the Penal Law provides a dual-criminality exception that permits prosecution, and cases are often triggered by digital evidence discovered during unrelated investigations rather than by a family complaint. The state ISP Omantel enables surveillance, and outing carries both social and criminal consequences. Foreign nationals convicted of a felony face mandatory deportation under Article 60 (permanent), with deportation of 3 to 15 years available for misdemeanours.

Oman bans legal gender recognition and explicitly bans gender-affirming healthcare, according to a joint stakeholder submission by Cairo 52 and White Tent dated 6 August 2025 to Oman's 4th-cycle Universal Periodic Review. The submission documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people, states that recent legislative developments have deepened criminalisation of gender expression, and reports that Oman has ignored earlier UPR recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access. It recommends ending criminalisation, adopting an anti-discrimination law, and permitting legal recognition.

Advocacy for LGBT rights is itself a criminal act in Oman, as in other Gulf countries; activists use social media aliases to protect their identities, with rare exceptions. Assembly and advocacy are restricted under the Civil Associations Law. A September 2013 proposal by Gulf Cooperation Council states to devise a test screening out gay foreigners was described by officials as a mere proposal and was not implemented, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking.
tangentialFactors:
Oman's 2018 Penal Code replaced earlier provisions; Human Rights Watch's regional report of 16 April 2018 records that the new code added a provision punishing any man who 'appears to dress in women's clothing', alongside a regional comparison to Kuwait's 2007 imitation law, and documents barriers to LGBT organising in Oman.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Oman was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying profile documents Oman's criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression.

Scholarly framing of Oman's legal-religious context appears in Shafiqa Ahmadi, 'Islam and Homosexuality: Religious Dogma, Colonial Rule, and the Quest for Belonging' (Journal of Civil Rights and Economic Development, 2012), which distinguishes homosexual acts from homosexual persons and notes that some Islamic countries criminalise acts, even by death, without criminalising identity.

outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Oman returned HTTP 403 at research time and could not be read directly; its content is characterised from the inventory note only.

The inventory does not state whether Oman's prison system houses convicted gender-nonconforming people in facilities matching their gender identity; this remains unresolved and not sourced.

The inventory provides no trans-specific homicide or violence rate for Oman, and no general homicide rate for comparison, so no trans-specific violence magnitude can be stated.

The 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council screening proposal is recorded as a proposal that officials said was never implemented; whether any related entry screening practice exists currently is not sourced here.
